In [[mathematics]] and [[numerical analysis]], the van Wijngaarden transformation is a variant on the [[Euler transform]] used to accelerate the convergence of an [[alternating series]].  

One algorithm to compute [[Euler transform|Euler's transform]] runs as follows: <blockquote>Compute a row of partial sums <math display=block>s_{0,k} = \sum_{n=0}^k(-1)^n a_n</math> and form rows of averages between neighbors <math display=block>s_{j+1,k} = \frac{s_{j,k}+s_{j,k+1}}2</math>  The first column <math>s_{j,0}</math> then contains the partial sums of the Euler transform.</blockquote>  

[[Adriaan van Wijngaarden]]'s contribution was to point out that it is better not to carry this procedure through to the very end, but to stop two-thirds of the way.<ref>[[Adriaan van Wijngaarden|A. van Wijngaarden]], in:  Cursus:  Wetenschappelijk Rekenen B, Proces Analyse, Stichting Mathematisch Centrum, (Amsterdam, 1965) pp. 51-60</ref> If  <math>a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{12}</math> are available, then <math>s_{8,4}</math> is almost always a better approximation to the sum than <math>s_{12,0}</math>.  In many cases the diagonal terms do not converge in one cycle so process of averaging is to be repeated with diagonal terms by bringing them in a row. (For example, this will be needed in a geometric series with ratio <math>-4</math>.) This process of successive averaging of the average of partial sum can be replaced by using the formula to calculate the diagonal term.  

For a simple-but-concrete example, recall the [[Leibniz formula for π]]: {{NumBlk|:|<math>1 - \frac 1 3 + \frac  1 5 -  \frac 1 7 + \cdots = \frac \pi 4 = 0.7853981\ldots</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}  The algorithm described above produces the following table:
